name: Buy Borrow Die Simulator
tag: See how buying assets, borrowing against them and passing them on could play out over time.

scenarios.title: Model a portfolio over 10 years
scenarios.ask: I hold ${value} in assets growing {growth} a year. If I borrow at {rate} instead of selling, what does it look like in 10 years?
steps: Projected value after 10 years with simple growth: ${=round(value * (1 + growth * 10 / 100))}.
Borrowed ${=round(value * ltv / 100)} today. Interest-only cost over 10 years: ${=round(value * ltv / 100 * rate / 100 * 10)}.
Showed how a step-up in basis at death can reset the taxable gain for heirs under current U.S. rules.

result.title: 10-year illustration
rows: Illustration only, not tax or financial advice

followups: Then the asset never outgrows the loan and you pay interest of about ${=round(value * ltv / 100 * rate / 100)} a year. Borrowing only makes sense if growth and income cover that cost over time.
Is the step-up in basis guaranteed?
It is part of current federal tax law, which can change. Estate size, state rules and how assets are titled all matter, so review your plan with a CPA and estate attorney.

scenarios.title: Stress test the loan
scenarios.ask: My ${value} portfolio carries a loan worth {loanpct} of its value. The lender calls at {call} loan-to-value. What price drop can I survive?
steps: Loan balance is ${=round(value * loanpct / 100)}, a loan-to-value of {loanpct}.
Applied a {drop} fall. Portfolio value becomes ${=round(value * (1 - drop / 100))}.
Loan-to-value after the drop: {=round(loanpct / max(1, 100 - drop) * 100, 1)}% against a {call} limit.
Worked out the largest drop before the lender's limit is reached.
followups: What does cash needed to cure mean?
It is how much of the loan you would need to pay down to get back under the {call} limit after the drop. Zero means you stay under the limit.
How do people lower this risk?
Common approaches are borrowing less, keeping a cash reserve, and spreading the loan across assets that don't move together. The simulator lets you test each one.

scenarios.title: Borrow or sell for living costs
scenarios.ask: I need ${need} this year. Compare selling assets with a {gain} gain versus borrowing at {rate}.

inputs.label: Share of sale that is gain

steps: Selling to raise ${need} creates a taxable gain of about ${=round(need * gain / 100)}.
Estimated federal tax at {taxrate}: ${=round(need * gain / 100 * taxrate / 100)}.
Borrowing ${need} at {rate} costs about ${=round(need * rate / 100)} a year in interest.
Shows how many years of interest equal the one-time tax bill.

result.title: Sell vs borrow
rows: Interest per year if you borrow
Years of interest to equal the tax
Federal estimate only; state tax not included

followups: No. Interest repeats every year while the tax is paid once. If you borrow for longer than about {=round(need * gain / 100 * taxrate / 100 / max(1, need * rate / 100), 1)} years, interest can cost more than the tax would have.
It is the top 20% federal long-term rate plus the 3.8% net investment income tax that applies at higher incomes. Your CPA can confirm which rate fits you.
